---
title: "Analyzing an Experiment You Already Ran"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(EDI)
```

Every other EDI vignette starts with EDI assigning treatment. Many analyses start
later than that. The experiment is over, treatment was assigned by someone else (a
randomization list, a sealed-envelope system, an online platform), and what you
have is a data frame: one row per subject, some covariates, a 0/1 treatment column
and an outcome.

EDI (Experimental Design and Inference) analyzes that data frame with the same
classes it uses everywhere else. The only change is in step 2 of the usual
four-step pattern (see [Get started](EDI.html)): instead of letting the design draw
the assignment, you hand it the assignment you already have.

1. **Construct the `Design` that matches how treatment was actually assigned**, with
   the same `n`, `prob_T` and blocks as the real experiment.
2. **Supply the observed treatment vector** with
   `assign_w_to_all_subjects(w_precomputed = w)`.
3. **Record the responses** with `add_all_subject_responses()`.
4. **Construct an `Inference` class** (or an `InferenceSuite`) and compute.

## Why the design class matters

A point estimate, a Wald interval or a likelihood-ratio test only looks at the data
you have. For those, the design class mostly affects how the covariates are stored.

Randomization inference is different. A randomization test asks: if treatment had no
effect, how unusual is the observed statistic among all the assignments the
experiment *could* have produced? EDI answers by redrawing `w` many times from the
design object's own randomization law, so that law has to be the one that was
really used. The bootstrap is affected in the same way for blocked designs, because
it resamples within blocks. If you declare complete randomization for an experiment
that was randomized within sites, the reference distribution includes assignments
that could never have happened, and the p-value is wrong.

So before writing any code, find out from the protocol or the randomization log:

| What was done | EDI design | What to set |
|---|---|---|
| A fixed number treated, all such allocations equally likely ("complete randomization") | `DesignFixediBCRD` | `prob_T = n_T / n`, so `round(n * prob_T)` is the number actually treated |
| An independent coin flip per subject; the number treated was random | `DesignFixedBernoulli` | `prob_T` = the coin's probability (often 0.5), not the realized fraction |
| Complete randomization within strata (site, sex, ...) | `DesignFixedBlocking` | `strata_cols` naming the stratum column(s), or `m` with one block ID per subject |
| Pairs formed first, one of each pair treated | `DesignFixedBinaryMatch` | see its help page |
| Not randomized (treatment chosen by subjects or clinicians) | `ObservationalDesign` | no `prob_T`; randomization inference is unavailable |

The remaining fixed designs in the
[reference index](https://kapelner.github.io/EDI/reference/index.html) all have
`assign_w_to_all_subjects(w_precomputed = )` too. If the experiment used a
covariate-adaptive or response-adaptive *sequential* procedure (Efron's biased
coin, Pocock-Simon minimization, KK matching on the fly), this article does not
apply: EDI's sequential designs assign each subject as they arrive and have no
argument for supplying a recorded assignment.

## A finished multi-site trial

Here is the kind of data frame this article is about. Eighty patients were enrolled
at four sites, twenty per site. At each site, ten were assigned to treatment by
complete randomization. BMI was not recorded for a few patients. The outcome is a
continuous score. The data are simulated, but the analysis below only uses the data
frame `trial`, exactly as if it had been read from a file.

```{r data}
set.seed(20261117)
n = 80
trial = data.frame(
  site   = rep(c("A", "B", "C", "D"), each = 20),
  age    = round(rnorm(n, 50, 10)),
  bmi    = round(rnorm(n, 28, 4), 1),
  smoker = rbinom(n, 1, 0.3)
)
trial$treated = unlist(lapply(1:4, function(s) sample(rep(0:1, each = 10))))
trial$bmi[sample(n, 6)] = NA
site_effect = c(A = 0, B = 6, C = 12, D = -6)
trial$score = 20 + 3 * trial$treated + 0.2 * trial$age + site_effect[trial$site] +
  rnorm(n, sd = 4)

head(trial)
table(trial$site, trial$treated)
```

Treatment was randomized within site, so the matching design is `DesignFixedBlocking`
with `strata_cols = "site"`. The covariate data frame passed to the design holds
only the covariates: no treatment column and no outcome.

```{r design}
X = trial[, c("site", "age", "bmi", "smoker")]

des = DesignFixedBlocking$new(n = n, response_type = "continuous", strata_cols = "site",
                              prob_T = 0.5, verbose = FALSE)
des$add_all_subjects_to_experiment(X)
des$assign_w_to_all_subjects(w_precomputed = trial$treated)
des$add_all_subject_responses(trial$score)

all(des$get_w() == trial$treated)
```

It is worth checking that the design reproduces the real randomization law. Each
column of `draw_ws_according_to_design()` is one assignment the design could have
produced; every one should treat ten patients at each site, as the real trial did.

```{r check-draws}
draws = des$draw_ws_according_to_design(5)
apply(draws, 2, function(w) tapply(w, trial$site, sum))
```

## Estimate, interval and p-value

`InferenceContinOLS` regresses the outcome on treatment and the covariates.

```{r ols}
inf = InferenceContinOLS$new(des, verbose = FALSE)
inf$num_cores = 1L

est = inf$compute_estimate()
ci = inf$compute_asymp_confidence_interval(alpha = 0.05)
p_wald = inf$compute_asymp_two_sided_pval()
est; ci; p_wald
```

The estimated treatment effect is `r round(est, 2)` points, with a 95% Wald interval
from `r round(ci[1], 2)` to `r round(ci[2], 2)`.

## Randomization test

The randomization test redraws `w` within sites `r` times, recomputes the statistic
for each draw, and compares the observed statistic with that reference
distribution. It needs no assumption about the distribution of the outcome. A real
analysis would use a larger `r`.

```{r rand}
inf$set_seed(1)
p_rand = inf$compute_rand_two_sided_pval(r = 500, show_progress = FALSE)
p_rand
```

The bootstrap also follows the blocks: by default it resamples patients within each
site.

```{r boot}
inf$set_seed(1)
inf$compute_bootstrap_confidence_interval(alpha = 0.05, B = 200, show_progress = FALSE)
```

## Every applicable analysis

`InferenceSuite` runs every inference class that applies to this design and
response type. As in the cookbooks, the call below runs only the asymptotic methods
and gives each class at most 15 seconds; drop `methods` for the full report,
including the randomization and bootstrap procedures, which takes minutes.

```{r suite}
suite = InferenceSuite$new(des)
res = suite$run_all_inference(screen = TRUE, plots = FALSE, num_cores = 1L,
                              methods = c("wald", "score", "lik_ratio"),
                              max_secs_per_class = 15)
```

## Covariates

### Choosing which covariates enter the model

By default, an inference class adjusts for every covariate in the design's
covariate matrix. Character and factor columns become dummy variables, so `site`
enters as three indicators:

```{r get-x}
head(des$get_X())
```

The `model_formula` argument of an inference class chooses a different
adjustment set. It is applied to the design's covariates (after imputation, see
below), and the treatment term is added for you.

```{r model-formula}
inf_age_site = InferenceContinOLS$new(des, model_formula = ~ age + site, verbose = FALSE)
inf_age_site$num_cores = 1L
inf_age_site$compute_estimate()
inf_age_site$compute_asymp_confidence_interval(alpha = 0.05)
```

Choose the adjustment set before looking at the results, ideally from the
analysis plan. Picking the covariates that give the smallest p-value invalidates
the p-value.

### Missing covariate values

Six patients have no BMI. Two design arguments control what happens:

- `missingness_method` decides how the gaps are handled. `"impute"` (the default)
  fills them in by random-forest imputation (`missRanger`) from the other covariates
  only, never the outcome or the treatment, so an imputed value cannot carry part of
  the treatment effect; it is seeded, so the same data always impute the same way.
  `"drop_column"` drops any
  covariate column with a missing value; `"error"` stops so that nothing is changed
  silently.
- `include_is_missing_as_a_new_feature` (default `TRUE`) adds a 0/1 indicator for
  each covariate with missing values. That is the `bmi_is_missing` column above.

Under the defaults, the model above used imputed BMI values plus the indicator. To
leave BMI out of the analysis instead:

```{r drop-column}
des_drop = DesignFixedBlocking$new(n = n, response_type = "continuous", strata_cols = "site",
                                   prob_T = 0.5, missingness_method = "drop_column",
                                   verbose = FALSE)
des_drop$add_all_subjects_to_experiment(X)
des_drop$assign_w_to_all_subjects(w_precomputed = trial$treated)
des_drop$add_all_subject_responses(trial$score)
colnames(des_drop$get_X())

inf_drop = InferenceContinOLS$new(des_drop, verbose = FALSE)
inf_drop$num_cores = 1L
inf_drop$compute_estimate()
```

Missing *outcomes* are a different problem. `add_all_subject_responses()` needs a
value for every subject, so subjects lost to follow-up have to be handled before
the data reach EDI (or, for a time-to-event outcome, recorded as censored, as in the
next section).

## A survival outcome with censoring

The `veteran` data in the survival package come from a randomized trial of two
chemotherapy regimens for lung cancer: `trt` is the regimen (1 standard, 2 test),
`time` is survival in days, and `status` is 0 for a censored patient.

```{r veteran}
vet = survival::veteran
table(vet$trt)
table(vet$status)
```

The data set's documentation says the trial was randomized but not how. Here we
assume complete randomization with the observed number on the test regimen. In a
real analysis this is the point to check the original report or the protocol. With
`DesignFixediBCRD`, the number treated in every redraw is `round(n * prob_T)`, so
setting `prob_T` to the observed fraction reproduces the observed count.

Censored patients are recorded as the interval `(y_L, Inf)`: `ys` is `NA` for them,
and `y_Ls`/`y_Rs` are `NA` for patients whose death time was observed.

```{r veteran-design}
w_vet = as.integer(vet$trt == 2)
cens = vet$status == 0

des_vet = DesignFixediBCRD$new(n = nrow(vet), response_type = "survival",
                               prob_T = mean(w_vet), verbose = FALSE)
des_vet$add_all_subjects_to_experiment(vet[, c("celltype", "karno", "diagtime", "age", "prior")])
des_vet$assign_w_to_all_subjects(w_precomputed = w_vet)
des_vet$add_all_subject_responses(
  ys   = ifelse(cens, NA, vet$time),
  y_Ls = ifelse(cens, vet$time, NA),
  y_Rs = ifelse(cens, Inf, NA)
)
colSums(des_vet$draw_ws_according_to_design(3))   # each redraw treats sum(w_vet) patients
```

A Cox model adjusted for the baseline covariates gives the log hazard ratio of the
test regimen, a likelihood-ratio interval and p-value, and a randomization test.

```{r veteran-cox}
inf_vet = InferenceSurvivalCoxPHRegr$new(des_vet, verbose = FALSE)
inf_vet$num_cores = 1L
log_hr = inf_vet$compute_estimate()
ci_vet = inf_vet$compute_lik_ratio_confidence_interval(alpha = 0.05)
log_hr; ci_vet
inf_vet$compute_lik_ratio_two_sided_pval()

inf_vet$set_seed(1)
inf_vet$compute_rand_two_sided_pval(r = 500, show_progress = FALSE)
```

The estimated hazard ratio is `r round(exp(log_hr), 2)`, with a 95% interval from
`r round(exp(ci_vet[1]), 2)` to `r round(exp(ci_vet[2]), 2)`: the data do not
distinguish the two regimens. More classes and procedures for this response type
are in `vignette("cookbook-survival")`.

## Pitfalls

### Declaring the wrong design

The design you declare has to be the one that generated `w`. To see what goes
wrong otherwise, analyze the multi-site trial a second time, declaring complete
randomization over all 80 patients and ignoring the sites. The unadjusted
difference in means (`InferenceAllSimpleAverageDiff`) shows the effect most
clearly, because it does not adjust for site.

```{r wrong-design}
des_wrong = DesignFixediBCRD$new(n = n, response_type = "continuous", prob_T = 0.5,
                                 verbose = FALSE)
des_wrong$add_all_subjects_to_experiment(X)
des_wrong$assign_w_to_all_subjects(w_precomputed = trial$treated)
des_wrong$add_all_subject_responses(trial$score)

rand_p = function(d) {
  i = InferenceAllSimpleAverageDiff$new(d, verbose = FALSE)
  i$num_cores = 1L
  i$set_seed(1)
  i$compute_rand_two_sided_pval(r = 1000, show_progress = FALSE)
}
p_right = rand_p(des)
p_wrong = rand_p(des_wrong)
c(blocked_by_site = p_right, ignoring_sites = p_wrong)
```

Both analyses use the same data and the same statistic. Declared correctly, the
randomization p-value is `r signif(p_right, 2)`; ignoring the sites, it is
`r signif(p_wrong, 2)`. Draws that ignore the sites can put most of the treated
patients in the high-scoring site C, so the reference distribution is far wider than
the one the real randomization could produce, and the test loses power. A mismatch
between the declared and the real design can also make a test reject too often;
either way, its p-value no longer means what it says.

Three related mistakes to check for:

- **Complete randomization with the wrong `prob_T`.** `DesignFixediBCRD` always
  treats `round(n * prob_T)` subjects in a redraw and does not compare that with the
  `w` you supply. If 30 of 80 were treated and you leave `prob_T = 0.5`, every redraw
  treats 40. Set `prob_T = mean(w)` and check `colSums()` of a few draws, as above.
- **Bernoulli versus complete randomization.** If each subject's assignment was an
  independent coin flip, use `DesignFixedBernoulli` with the coin's probability;
  its redraws let the number treated vary, as it did in the real experiment.
- **Data that were not randomized.** If treatment was chosen rather than
  randomized, no design reproduces the assignment mechanism. `ObservationalDesign`
  accepts the data and supports estimates and the plain nonparametric bootstrap, but
  randomization inference refuses to run, and the estimate is causal only under
  assumptions about confounding that EDI cannot check.

### Stratified and blocked experiments

- **Name the strata.** For `DesignFixedBlocking`, pass the stratum column(s) as
  `strata_cols`. Character and factor columns form one block per level. A numeric
  column may instead be cut into quantile bins, which almost certainly does not
  match the real strata, so convert numeric stratum codes with `factor()` first
  (`?DesignFixedBlocking` gives the exact rule). If the
  strata are not columns of `X`, or you want full control, pass `m`, one block ID
  per subject.
- **Unequal block sizes.** `equal_block_sizes = TRUE` is the default. With strata of
  different sizes the design then errors, not when the data are added but the first
  time the blocks are used (a redraw, a randomization test or an inference fit). Real
  trials rarely have equal strata; set `equal_block_sizes = FALSE`.
- **Different allocation ratios across strata.** The design's redraws treat
  `floor(N * prob_T)` or `ceiling(N * prob_T)` subjects in a block of size `N`. If
  the real trial used a different ratio in different strata, the redraws do not
  reproduce it. Check `draw_ws_according_to_design()` against the observed counts
  per stratum before trusting a randomization test.
- **Blocks and the regression model.** Randomization tests, the bootstrap and the
  jackknife respect the blocks. Regression classes such as `InferenceContinOLS` do
  not add block effects on their own; the blocks enter the model only if the
  stratum column is one of the covariates, as `site` is here. If the proportion
  treated differs across strata, adjusting for the strata is required for an
  unbiased estimate; see `?DesignFixedBlocking`.
